newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU warns Asian bars threaten WTO financial pact.
newsitem.headline: EU warns Asian bars threaten WTO financial pact.

text.p: The European Union warned on Thursday that signs key Asian countries were moving to tighten up curbs on foreign investment in their financial service industries could sink a global pact now under negotiation.
The warning, which specifically pointed to Malaysia, was issued as members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) began two days of talks on the deal, facing a deadline of December 12 for completion.

Malaysian moves aimed at forcing foreign firms currently in its financial services market to disinvest "are exactly the opposite of what we are trying to do," senior EU negotiator Hans Friedrich Beseler told a news briefing.

"This could be a serious problem if other countries follow suit, and there are signs that Malaysia is unfortunately not alone....that Indonesia, and perhaps others, may also be going in that direction," Beseler said.

Earlier this week, U.S. officials also warned that Asian, and Latin American, reluctance to open up markets for banking, securities and insurance could wreck any hopes for a deal -- which big powers argue will benefit developing countries.

Senior U.S. officials are planning to tour key Asian capitals -- including Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Seoul and Delhi -- next month in a drive to win wider openings for outside firms in the multi-billion dollar sector.

The United States -- which has the world's largest national market for financial services and is therefore vital for a global deal -- walked away from an agreement in June 1995, saying emerging economies were not offering enough.

But this week, following new offers from the EU and Japan, it tabled a package offering to throw open the sector in the U.S. to all comers on the most-favoured-nation (MFN) principle, the basic underpinning of WTO accords.
Beseler on Thursday hailed the latest U.S. offer as "a major and very welcome step" that gave new impetus to the negotiations, expected to begin in earnest in the autumn.

When the 1995 talks were on the verge of collapse after the U.S. pullout, the EU convinced other WTO members to shape an interim deal keeping their offers on the table, but that pact runs out at the end of this year.

Beseler, Director-General for commercial policy in the European Commission's external relations department, also said the Japanese offer included "significant improvements" which met many EU concerns.

He indicated that, although the latest Canadian package did not go much further than its offer in the 1995 talks, Brussels was ready to wait for the new government in Ottawa to settle in and make more far-reaching proposals.

But he said South Korea was "not as forthcoming as we would like it to be", while Brazil -- the major financial service power in Latin America -- was showing reluctance to allow in new banks and insurance companies from outside.
The EU welcomed improved offers from Australia, Bahrain, Hong Kong, Hungary, Norway and Switzerland. But others would now have to respond to put a deal in sight.
"We need a high level of offers or there will be a danger that the negotiations will fail and we will lose even the benefits of the temporary deal done in 1995," Beseler added.

If that happened, he said, "WTO members will miss out on the benefits of private investment providing the life-blood which can sustain our economies and promote worldwide development and competitiveness."
